rationale: IBD consistently goes with lower gut microbial diversity (dysbiosis), and a random forest can't easily rebuild a whole-community summary from separate genus splits. This adds alpha-diversity features to the genus relative abundances: Shannon and inverse Simpson at OTU and genus level, plus OTU and genus richness estimated by rarefaction to a common depth so that study sequencing depth doesn't skew it.

The four studies differ in sequencing depth, 16S region and protocol, so the same relative-abundance value for a genus means different things in different studies. I'm converting each genus abundance to its percentile rank among samples from the same study. This is label-free and uses only the `study` metadata. Rank normalisation is a common way to correct microbiome batch effects. I'm also adding study one-hot indicators so the forest keeps the per-study case/control base rates.

Right now the code takes only the genus field when it aggregates, so every unclassified-genus OTU (`g__`) from every family lands in one meaningless "g__" bin. It also never looks at the family level, where IBD dysbiosis shows up strongly (loss of Ruminococcaceae/Lachnospiraceae, gain of Enterobacteriaceae). This change aggregates by the full lineage prefix at both family and genus level, so unclassified genera stay inside their own family, and keeps the within-study percentile ranks, study one-hot and random forest unchanged.

Many genera are rare or show up in only one study because of differences in 16S region, classifier or protocol. Their within-study ranks are mostly ties at zero and noise, yet they still get drawn into the forest's random feature subsets. This change keeps only genera seen in at least 10% of samples in at least two studies. The filter is label-free, uses only the study metadata, and should leave a smaller set of taxa that transfer across studies, which should make the forest's splits more reliable.

IBD dysbiosis is a broad shift, with many taxa moving together in the same direction (commensal Firmicutes go down, Proteobacteria go up), so the signal is largely additive. The random forest picks this up only through scattered threshold splits. I'm adding an L2 logistic regression on the same within-study rank features and averaging its probabilities with the forest's. The regularization strength is tuned by grouped inner CV on the training fold only.

Gevers 2014, the RISK study in this pool, defined a microbial dysbiosis index for IBD. It is the log-ratio of taxa that increase in IBD (Enterobacteriaceae, Pasteurellaceae, Veillonellaceae, Fusobacteriaceae) to taxa that decrease (Erysipelotrichales, Bacteroidales, Clostridiales). This change adds that index and a second log-ratio, butyrate producers (Faecalibacterium + Roseburia) vs Enterobacteriaceae. Both are percentile-ranked within study like the other features. The forest can't easily build a sum-of-many-taxa contrast from single-genus splits, and a log-ratio is unaffected by sequencing depth.

With `method="average"`, all of a study's zero-abundance samples share one mid-rank. That value depends on how prevalent the genus is in that study (about 0.35 if 70% of the study's samples are zeros, 0.05 if 10% are). So "genus absent" maps to a different number in each study, and one forest split mixes absent samples from one study with present samples from another. Pinning zeros to 0 keeps the within-study ordering. It also gives the forest a presence/absence threshold that works the same way in every study, which matters because losing commensal taxa outright is a core IBD dysbiosis signal.

I'm replacing the random forest with 1000 extremely randomized trees (ExtraTrees, min_samples_leaf=2). The rank features are bounded in [0,1], have many ties and noisy study-specific cut points, so random split thresholds and averaging over more trees should give a smoother score that transfers better across the grouped folds; that matters because IBD dysbiosis is a broad, diffuse shift rather than a few sharp cut-offs.

IBD dysbiosis is a departure from the healthy community state as a whole (Halfvarson 2017 measured it as median distance to non-IBD reference samples). A forest can't build that from single-genus splits. In `fit_predict` I add a dysbiosis score: each sample's median L1 distance, on the within-study genus ranks, to the training-fold controls from the same study. Controls from the same subject are excluded for training items, so the score never sees the sample's own label.

The current dysbiosis score only measures how far a sample sits from healthy controls, but IBD communities also share a characteristic disease state (for example Proteobacteria bloom and loss of commensals). So I'm adding a matched score: the median L1 distance on within-study ranks to training-fold IBD cases from the same study, excluding the sample's own subject. I'm also adding the control-minus-case difference, which acts as a smooth, study-aware nearest-centroid contrast that the trees can split on directly.

A core sign of IBD dysbiosis is that taxa a healthy gut almost always carries go missing. I'm adding a "core-microbiome loss" score: the share of genera missing from a sample, with each genus weighted by how common it is among same-study training controls. The sample's own subject is left out of the prevalence calculation. Building the reference from same-study controls keeps it batch-aware, and the trees cannot assemble this whole-community presence/absence summary from single-genus splits.

Within-study percentile ranks of phylum, class and family abundances are added alongside the genus ranks. The genus aggregation and the dysbiosis score stay the same. Higher taxonomic levels are classified more consistently across studies that use different 16S regions and classifiers. They also hold the main IBD signals directly, Proteobacteria/Enterobacteriaceae up and Firmicutes/Ruminococcaceae down, which the trees otherwise have to piece together from many sparse genus splits.

The raw dysbiosis distance has a different scale in each study, because studies detect different numbers of genera and differ in depth. A single tree threshold therefore means different things across the pooled studies. I add a calibrated version that follows Halfvarson's reference-percentile idea: the sample's percentile among same-study training controls' own leave-subject-out dysbiosis scores, with the sample's own subject excluded. The result is a batch-free "how abnormal for this study" score.

In IBD, blooms of a few taxa such as Enterobacteriaceae or Bacteroides push down the relative abundance of every other genus purely through compositional closure. The within-study ranks of relative abundance therefore partly reflect the bloom rather than real loss of each commensal. I'm ranking robust-CLR values instead: the log of each nonzero abundance minus the mean log over that sample's nonzero genera, as in DEICODE. This is scale-invariant and does not depend on pseudocounts or richness, and absent genera are still pinned to rank 0. The trees and the dysbiosis distance then see per-genus abundances relative to each sample's own typical taxon level.

The current dysbiosis score is the median distance to all same-study controls. That mostly reflects how varied the controls are, and it misses healthy controls that cluster into several enterotype-like groups. I'm adding a local-outlier version: the mean L1 distance on within-study genus ranks to the 10 nearest same-study training controls, still excluding the sample's own subject. A healthy sample should sit close to some control group, while an IBD community should be far from every healthy group.

The trees will now see each genus as a percentile of that study's healthy-control distribution, following Gibbons et al. 2018 ("percentile normalization" for pooling case-control microbiome studies). This replaces the percentile among all of the study's samples. The current ranks shift with each study's case/control ratio, so "median" means something different in a case-heavy study like RISK than in a control-heavy one. With healthy controls as the reference, a value of 0.5 means "typical healthy for this study" in every study. To avoid leakage, a training item's own subject is left out of its reference. Absent taxa stay pinned to 0. If a study has fewer than 5 training controls, the old within-study rank is used. The dysbiosis score is unchanged.

The dysbiosis score is the only feature still computed on within-study ranks of all samples, so it still depends on each study's case/control mix. This change computes it on the healthy-control percentiles the trees already use, so "distance from health" is measured in the same frame in every study. That puts Halfvarson's dysbiosis score and the Gibbons percentile normalization on one consistent scale, and the same-subject exclusion is kept.

Studies differ a lot in case/control ratio. Right now the trees can learn those base rates from any study-specific taxon (for example a genus only one protocol detects), which wastes splits on study identity instead of disease signal. This change trains the ExtraTrees with sample weights that balance cases and controls within each study, so the trees model only within-study disease likelihood. It then adds each study's training prior log-odds back on the logit scale, an explicit Bayes prior shift, so the pooled ranking still uses the study base rates.

With `max_features="sqrt"`, each split only sees about 5% of the roughly 300+ features, so the few strong signals (the dysbiosis score, study indicators, Enterobacteriaceae/Faecalibacterium percentiles) are rarely among the split candidates and get swamped by sparse, noisy genera. This change picks the ExtraTrees `max_features` from {sqrt, 0.1, 0.25} by grouped 3-fold inner CV on the training fold only, so the data decides how strongly to favour the dominant dysbiosis axes over the diffuse genus signal.

Percentile normalisation against controls caps every value above the healthiest-range maximum at 1.0. That throws away the size of IBD blooms: Enterobacteriaceae at 10× the healthy maximum looks the same as a value just over it. This change extends the percentile past 1 by log10(abundance / max of same-study controls), with the sample's own subject left out of that maximum. The trees can then split on how far a taxon blooms beyond the study's healthy range, while the scale inside the healthy range stays as it is.
